engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Opening Principle #1: Control the Centre
chess.body: Place pawns on e4/d4 (White) or e5/d5 (Black). Pieces control more squares from the centre. A pawn on e4 controls d5 and f5. A pawn on the edge controls only 1 square. Open with 1.e4 or 1.d4 and you immediately claim space. This is the foundation of all chess strategy.

book.author: Clayton Christensen
book.chapter: Why Great Companies Fail at Exactly the Right Moment
book.lesson: Christensen's paradox: the best-managed companies, doing everything right — listening to customers, investing in quality, maximising margins — are the most vulnerable to disruption. Disruptive technologies start at the bottom of the market (cheaper, simpler, worse performance) serving customers who don't exist yet. They improve over time until they're good enough for mainstream customers. By then, it's too late for incumbents to respond. Nokia had better technology than Apple in 2007. Blockbuster had better retail locations than Netflix. They failed not despite their excellence but because of it — their success made them unable to cannibalise themselves.
book.key_quote: Excellence in executing today's business model can blind you to the business model that will replace it.
book.action: Ask about your industry: what is the simpler, cheaper, 'worse' solution that currently serves the bottom of the market? Could it eventually serve everyone?
crux: Well-managed companies fail precisely by doing what good management prescribes.
Sustaining innovations improve products for existing customers. Incumbents win these reliably.
Disruptive innovations start worse on the metrics incumbents value, and win anyway.
Disruption enters at the low end or in a new market, where incumbent margins look unattractive.
Listening closely to your best customers pushes you away from disruptive bets. Rationally.
Resource dependence: customers and investors, not managers, effectively allocate the resources.
Small markets cannot solve the growth needs of large companies, so large companies skip them.
Technology supply often outruns demand — products overshoot what users need, opening the low end.
The basis of competition shifts over time: function → reliability → convenience → price.
You cannot analyse markets that do not yet exist. Discovery-driven planning, not forecasting.
Disruption must be housed in an independent organisation small enough to be excited by a small win.
Failure early and cheaply is the plan, because the first strategy will be wrong.
learnings: Doing everything right is not protection when the game changes underneath.
The customers who fund you today are the reason you miss tomorrow.
A market too small to matter now is the only place disruption can start.
Cost structure determines which opportunities look attractive. It is destiny.
examples: Disk drives: every generational shift from 14-inch to 1.8-inch killed the leader, though each new size was initially worse on capacity.
Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975 and could not commit to it without cannibalising film margins.
Mini-mills started with low-grade rebar that integrated steel mills were happy to abandon, then moved up until they took the whole market.
adapt: A free Telegram bot is the low-end disruption of paid research. That is the position to hold, not apologise for.
Codex at $47 looks unattractive next to consulting rates. That is exactly why it has room.
Don't let existing dashboard users dictate the roadmap if the measured edge points elsewhere.
Keep experiments in separate ledgers — the APEX poly engine on its own books, so a small bet stays a small bet.

interview_tech.q: Explain deferred tax to a board member in 60 seconds.
interview_tech.a: Accounting profit and taxable profit are computed under different rules, so tax paid this year rarely matches tax on this year's reported profit. Deferred tax records the future consequence of that gap. The classic retail example is accelerated capital allowances on fit-out: you get the tax relief early, so you owe more tax later — that future obligation sits as a deferred tax liability. It is not cash and it is not a provision for a dispute; it is timing. Say that last sentence, because it is what they are actually worried about.

interview_tech.q: How do you measure promotional effectiveness properly?
interview_tech.a: Incremental margin, not uplift. Take the sales during the promotion, subtract what the baseline would have been without it, subtract the margin given away on units that would have sold at full price anyway, and subtract any cannibalisation of adjacent full-price lines. The result is often negative for deep discounts on already-popular SKUs. Use a control group of comparable stores where operationally possible — without a counterfactual, every promotion looks successful because sales always rise.

interview_soft.q: What questions do you have for us?
interview_soft.a: Never none. Ask things that reveal you are evaluating them: what does the first 12 months look like for whoever takes this; what is the finance function currently not able to answer that the board keeps asking; how is the relationship between finance and the commercial teams today; and why is the role open. The last one is the most informative and the least asked. Avoid salary and benefits at first interview.

interview_soft.q: Describe a situation where you had incomplete information and had to decide anyway.
interview_soft.a: Forecasting and provisioning are full of these. Structure: what you knew, what you could not know in the time available, the cost of waiting, the assumption you took and why, and how you made the assumption visible rather than burying it. The mark of seniority is deciding with 70% of the information and saying explicitly what would change your mind — say that phrase.

cfo_field.q: Read the cash flow statement first. Always.
cfo_field.a: P&L is an opinion, cash is a fact. Open any set of accounts at the cash flow statement, compare operating cash flow to EBITDA over three years, and look at the gap. A business converting 90%+ of EBITDA to operating cash is real. One converting 50% has its profit sitting in working capital or is capitalising something it should be expensing. That one ratio finds more problems than any variance pack.
cfo_field.who: The first thing to check, every time

cfo_field.q: Scenario planning beats a single budget, and costs less than it sounds.
cfo_field.a: Three cases — base, downside, upside — with the two or three variables that actually move the outcome, not thirty. In retail that is usually like-for-like growth, gross margin, and rent renewals. The value is not the numbers; it is that the board has already discussed the downside before it arrives, so the conversation when it does is about the response rather than about whether it is happening.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early piece activity: develop knights to f6/e5 and bishops before pushing ...c6; avoid passive pawn moves that waste time.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early pawn structure: after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6, develop knights before pushing ...f5; reduce average move time from 30 s to ≤15 s to avoid time‑pressure errors.
lichess_games.standout: Decided on the clock, not the board — the position was still playable when time ran out.

lichess_summary.session_summary: AKK_010 dominates the current pool, but the 100 % win rate masks a glaring opening flaw: you repeatedly allow Black to equalize with the early …c5‑d5 pawn break in the English, leaving you with cramped pieces and a passive king‑side. Switch to a more assertive setup—play 1.c4 c5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.Nf3 Nf6 6.0‑0 0‑0 and seize the centre with d4 on move 7, forcing Black onto the back foot. Until you purge the c5‑d5 escape route, every opponent who spots it will turn your “perfect” record into a collapse; drill the d4‑e4 break daily until it becomes second nature.

lichess_puzzle.tip: Lure the king or a key piece onto a bad square with a sacrifice.
